question.worked_solution:
Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
{F}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*

We wish to compute ${P}^{′}(t),$ where

$$
P(t)={\int }_{-1}^{1}(x+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Differentiating under the integral sign, we get

$$
{P}^{′}(t)={\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{∂}{∂t}[(x+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))^{2}]\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, let's compute the partial derivative with respect to $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂t}[(x+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))^{2}] & =2(x+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\cdot \frac{∂}{∂t}(x+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)) \\  & =2(x+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(t) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)(x+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this back into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(t) & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)(x+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t){\int }_{-1}^{1}(x+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's evaluate the remaining integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(x+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-1}^{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{-1}^{1}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\cdot x{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =0+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{P}^{′}(t)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$
